results.title: GPU prices explained | Intelaris
results.author: Intelaris Research
highlights:
Published Oct 9, 2026

## Price per GPU-hour

Cloud providers quote GPU capacity per GPU and hour. A server with eight GPUs costs eight times the GPU-hour price per hour.

Storage, outbound data transfer and support are usually charged separately.

## Pricing models

On-demand: billed by the hour, no commitment. Reserved: fixed capacity for one or three years at a lower price per hour.

Spot: unused capacity at a discount that the provider can reclaim. Community and marketplace: capacity from third parties, with varying reliability.

## Location, currency and availability

The same GPU costs different amounts in different regions. Providers quote in different currencies, for example USD, EUR or CHF.

A list price does not guarantee available capacity. AI Compute Prices shows availability where the source reports it.

## Spread in the market

For the H100, on-demand prices range from USD 2.65 EUR 2.38 CHF 2.20 to USD 14.38 EUR 12.92 CHF 11.93 per GPU-hour, with a median of USD 3.89 EUR 3.50 CHF 3.23, as of Nov 11, 2026.

As of Nov 11, 2026, 21:05 UTC Source: public price lists and pricing APIs of the providers Converted at ECB reference rates of Nov 11, 2026 Method

Nebius prints the rates in its document Compute pricing in Nebius AI Cloud. The page says on-demand prices for B300, B200, H200, and H100 changed on 1 October 2026, and that from 8 October 2026 the preemptible price on several of those platforms is a dynamic spot rate, displayed as a floor. The dollar figures on that page are before tax. The billing unit is one second and the pricing unit is one hour, so thirty minutes is half the hourly rate. A stopped virtual machine is not charged for the GPU. The bars are the on-demand rates read on 10 October 2026. The 8 October note on that page is a preemptible floor, and it is not drawn. The line above the bars is what an H100 hour has cost across the months a posted rate could be read.

NVIDIA B300 NVLink is 9.50 dollars for one GPU-hour, with a preemptible floor of 0.99 dollars. Before 1 October the same block lists 7.85 dollars on demand. NVIDIA B200 NVLink is 8.50 dollars for one GPU-hour. The page ties one platform id to us-central1 and another to me-west1, at the same on-demand rate, with a preemptible floor of 0.99 dollars. Before 1 October that block lists 7.15 dollars. NVIDIA H200 NVLink is 5.40 dollars, in eu-north1, eu-north2, eu-west1, and us-central1, with a preemptible floor of 0.79 dollars. Before 1 October it lists 4.50 dollars. NVIDIA H100 NVLink is 4.50 dollars, and the page says that platform is only in eu-north1. The preemptible floor is 0.79 dollars. Before 1 October it lists 3.85 dollars.

...

Lambda's instance page, opened the same day, lists the chip, the onboard memory, the vCPUs, and a price per GPU-hour, plus applicable tax. The B200 SXM6 row with 180 GB and 208 vCPUs is 6.69 dollars. The H100 SXM row with 80 GB and 208 vCPUs is 3.99 dollars. The A100 SXM row with 80 GB and 240 vCPUs is 2.79 dollars. The page groups further rows under smaller instance sizes. B200 SXM6 appears again at 6.79, 6.89, and 6.99 dollars, next to 104, 52, and 26 vCPUs. H100 SXM on those rows is 4.09, 4.19, and 4.29 dollars. An H100 PCIe row with 80 GB and 26 vCPUs is 3.29 dollars. A GH200 row with 96 GB is 2.29 dollars. Under the B200 section the page says the instances start at 6.69 dollars, and it says the part offers up to three times the training and fifteen times the inference of H100. It does not say how many tokens that hour produces.

...

A spot floor is not the on-demand rate. Nebius says the preemptible price can change as often as every fifteen minutes, that it stays at least one cent under the on-demand rate, and that the number on the documentation page is a minimum. The phrase is "from 0.79" or "from 0.99", not the charge a running job will see. The on-demand column is the figure a reader can compare next month without logging into a console.

An H100 hour has not moved in one smooth line, and the two rates on the chart are different offers. The SXM5 pay-as-you-go hour was $4.85 from November 2023 through July 2024, and $3.50 on 15 September 2024. The later NVLink hour was $2.95 from October 2025 through May 2026, $3.85 from 1 June 2026, and $4.50 from 1 October 2026. The months between September 2024 and November 2025 are left empty. The posted offer changed, and those in-between months were not in the copies read for this brief. A third quote, $2.118 for the GPU alone with the processor and memory billed beside it, is not drawn.

The useful update is the dated move on the Nebius page itself. From 1 October 2026 the on-demand H100 line goes from 3.85 to 4.50 dollars, the H200 line from 4.50 to 5.40, the B200 line from 7.15 to 8.50, and the B300 line from 7.85 to 9.50. Those four pairs are on one document, with the old rate left in place under a "before" heading. Lambda's instance rows do not carry a date. The 6.69 and 3.99 dollar figures are what that URL showed on 10 October 2026, and a revision should open the URL again rather than treat them as a contract.

results.title: NVIDIA H100, H200, B200, B300 Prices 2026: Buy or Rent
highlights:
NVIDIA does not publish any official prices for its data center GPUs. The figures in circulation come from analyst estimates, executive statements and resellers' list prices. Here is what we know as of October 2026, source by source, and what it means for a business that wants to run its own AI.

...

## Hourly rental prices in 2026

Public prices recorded on October 14, 2026, per GPU per hour, excluding tax:

| GPU | European clouds | Neoclouds | Hyperscalers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | OVHcloud €2.80; Scaleway (PCIe) from €2.86 | Lambda $3.99; Nebius $4.50 | AWS Capacity Blocks $5.97 |
| H200 | OVHcloud €5.25 | Nebius $5.40; CoreWeave $6.31 | AWS Capacity Blocks $7.90 |
| B200 | — | Lambda $6.69; Nebius $8.50; CoreWeave $8.60 | Google Cloud about $8.06; AWS Capacity Blocks $14.21 |
| B300 | Scaleway from €7.50 (8-GPU configuration) | Nebius $9.50 | AWS Capacity Blocks $16.15 |

The trend has reversed. Between 2024 and 2025, rental prices fell: according to Silicon Data, the median price of an H100 at the hyperscalers went from about $9.34 to $6.26 per hour, and AWS cut its H100 prices by 44% in June 2025. Since then, prices have been climbing again: according to SemiAnalysis, a one-year contract on an H100 rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per hour between October 2025 and March 2026, an increase of about 40%. AWS raised its Capacity Blocks prices by about 15% in January 2026, then by about 20% in July.

## Why prices are rising in 2026

- Memory. TrendForce observed a rise of about 20% in HBM3e prices and a surge in DRAM contract prices, with DRAM revenue jumping 59.5% in the second quarter of 2026.
- Demand exceeds supply. In April 2026, SemiAnalysis described on-demand capacity as sold out across all GPU types. In August, NVIDIA's CFO warned that supply would remain a bottleneck at least until the end of its fiscal year 2028.
- Announced price increases. According to Bloomberg, NVIDIA warned its customers of increases of more than 15% in many cases for Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell systems delivered in early 2027, due to the cost of memory.

The new Vera Rubin generation has been ramping up production since August 2026. But do not count on it to bring H100 and H200 prices down in the short term: SemiAnalysis notes that the industry expected Hopper prices to fall with the arrival of Blackwell, and that “the opposite happened”.

## What the hourly rate does not tell you

4. Reserved terms. For multi-month commitments on B200/B300, reserved pricing is quoted separately and depends on term length, location and interconnect. Nodus handles these through Reserved Compute.

results.title: H100 and B200 Cloud GPU Hourly Rates: October 2026 Pricing Curve | SpecForge
results.author: SpecForge Editorial Team
highlights:
1. On-demand H100 80GB cloud rentals ranged $1.71 to $10.98 per GPU-hour across 52 tracked providers as of October 2026, with the cheapest listing at Gcore and a market median near $3.23.
2. Last-released GPUs (B200/B300/MI300X/RTX 5090) saw median prices climb from $2.12 to $4.72 per GPU-hour between October 2024 and September 2026.

...

Across 52 providers tracked on October 11, 2026, NVIDIA H100 80GB on-demand rentals spanned $1.71 per GPU-hour at Gcore to $10.98 at the top of the hyperscaler band, with a market median of $3.23 per GPU-hour and a separate H100 SXM listing from $2.27/hr [S1][S10].

Last-released GPUs (B200, B300, MI300X, RTX 5090) saw their on-demand median rise from $2.12 per GPU-hour in October 2024 to $4.72 in September 2026, while the Modern cohort (H100/H200/A100/L40S/RTX 4090/A10G/T4/L4) moved only $1.35 to $1.45 over the same window [S3].

...

GetDeploying's index of 5,225 listings across 85 providers put the cheapest H100 80GB listing at $1.71 per GPU-hour (Gcore on-demand), against a 12-month trend of +8% [S1]. Separately, the Silicon Data GPU Rental Index recorded an isolated H100 spike of +10% in four weeks, from $2.00/hr on December 9, 2025 to $2.20/hr on January 6, 2026, with A100 and B200 flat over the same window [S5].

That spike ran counter to a multi-year normalization: H100 hourly rates fell from roughly $8/hr in early 2024 to a $1.50-$3.00/hr range by late 2025 across specialist providers, and H100 lead times compressed from over 50 weeks in 2023 to shorter delivery windows in 2024 [S5]. The October 2026 cross-provider range of $1.71 to $10.98 per GPU-hour now straddles both the discount end (boutique clouds, neoclouds, marketplace hosts) and the premium hyperscaler tier [S1][S4].

## B200, B300, GB200 and GB300 Rate Cards

The Blackwell generation carries a steep premium: B200 180GB lists from $3.75 per GPU-hour at Packet.ai with a $6.69 median, B300 288GB starts at $4.99 with a $7.87 median, and GB200 186GB starts at $10.50 with a $16.00 median across five providers [S1][S3]. The Grace Blackwell Ultra GB300 288GB tops the table at $18.00 per GPU-hour on Oracle Cloud, and Vast.ai's October 2026 live snapshot shows B200 at a $6.00 floor and $7.50 median, with H200 NVL at $3.71/$4.25 and H200 at $4.37/$5.00 [S1][S6].

Reserved versus on-demand spreads are GPU-specific: B300's reserved median is $5.71 against $7.87 on-demand, H100 has a tight $0.13 gap ($3.10 reserved vs $3.23 on-demand), and MI300X actually inverts the pattern, with reserved at $3.39 above its $2.91 on-demand median [S3]. For engineering procurement, the on-demand column is the safe reference; reserved medians combine mixed commitment terms and cannot be read as a same-provider discount [S3].

results.title: The Cheapest H100 Is Out of Stock: What 25 Clouds of GPU Pricing Data Shows | beCloudReady
results.author: Chandan Kumar
highlights:
We track hourly GPU prices across 25 clouds every night. The cheapest H100 on our list is out of stock, and most providers do not publish stock at all. Here is what the data shows and how we handle it.

On 14 October 2026 the lowest H100 price in our tracker was $1.66 per GPU-hour, listed by Latitude. That row is marked out of stock. The cheapest H100 that a provider says you can rent right now is $3.30 per GPU-hour, at Scaleway. That is almost double.

...

GPU Price is a free tracker we run for the data and AI teams we train. A scraper runs every night and publishes on-demand, per-GPU-hour prices from public pricing APIs and catalogs. No login, no scraping behind a form.

...

## What the data shows on 14 October

Median per-GPU-hour price of the offers in the tracker (not matched by instance size, so read these as a market snapshot rather than a benchmark):

| GPU | Offers | Providers | Lowest listed | Median | Highest listed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | 50 | 17 | $1.66 (Latitude, out of stock) | $3.25 | $10.00 (Oracle) |
| H200 | 21 | 10 | $2.25 (Excess Supply, out of stock) | $5.29 | $10.60 (Azure) |
| B200 | 17 | 9 | $3.74 (BoostRun, out of stock) | $7.79 | $14.24 (AWS) |
| A100 80GB | 45 | 14 | $1.35 (Excess Supply, in stock) | $1.98 | $4.10 (Azure) |
| L40S | 46 | 12 | $0.69 (BoostRun, out of stock) | $1.70 | $7.58 (AWS) |

...

1. The cheapest listing is usually not rentable. For H100, H200, B200 and L40S the lowest listed price is marked out of stock. For H100, 27 of the 50 offers are out of stock, 3 are in stock and 20 are unknown. A ranking that ignores this tells you to go to a provider that has nothing to sell you.

...

- Unknown stock is not available stock. For H100, 20 of 50 offers have no stock data. The cheapest in-stock H100 we can verify is $3.30, but a direct provider with no stock signal could be cheaper and rentable.
- Marketplace prices can include a markup. Shadeform resells capacity from other clouds. A marketplace price may differ from the same provider's own price page, and the marketplace may list a provider that also appears elsewhere.
- On-demand only. Spot, reserved and committed-use prices are excluded. They can change the ranking.
- Stock changes within hours. The snapshot is nightly. Treat it as where to look first, not as a reservation.
- Per-GPU price is not total cost. Egress, storage, minimum commitments and setup time are not in the number.

results.title: AI Compute Cost Outlook: Quarterly Briefing · AgentFlare
highlights:
### Pricing is high at the hyperscalers, discounted elsewhere

As of early November, H100 on-demand pricing ranged from roughly $6.88 per GPU-hour at AWS to $11.06 at Google Cloud, versus approximately $3.90–$6.16 across major neoclouds. [5] H200 pricing reached $10.60 per hour on Google Cloud, while B200 capacity was generally available through flexible-start or committed products rather than standard on-demand listings. [4] 

The spread is economically material: hyperscaler list prices averaged nearly twice GPU-cloud medians across H100, H200, and B200 instances. [1] This creates a strong incentive for workload migration, capacity brokering, and multicloud arbitrage—particularly for inference jobs with predictable utilization.

### Effective cost is falling through commitments and utilization

Reservation economics are increasingly decisive. One-year commitments reduce median GPU pricing by about 21%, while three-year commitments cut it by approximately 48% versus on-demand rates. [1] Google’s three-year H100 commitment was listed at $4.86 per GPU-hour, compared with an $11.06 on-demand rate; its H200 equivalent was $4.65 versus $10.60. [4] 

Spot pricing can be dramatically lower—up to 91% below on-demand in some Google configurations—but availability and interruption risk make it unsuitable as the sole basis for distributed training capacity. [4] The next quarters should therefore see more hybrid scheduling: committed capacity for critical training, spot for checkpointable jobs, and neocloud overflow for inference.

...

Token-level cost compression will come primarily from higher utilization, quantization, batching, speculative decoding, and model specialization—not simply lower GPU prices. For example, self-hosting a 120B-class model on eight B200s becomes competitive with a $0.60-per-million-output-token API at roughly 33% sustained utilization under Google flexible-start pricing, rising to about 58% under AWS on-demand economics. [4]

...

### Outlook: lower effective prices, firm premium hardware

Expect advertised hyperscaler GPU rates to remain sticky through the next two quarters, with selective increases where supply is tight—AWS raised several U.S. GPU configurations by about 15% in October after earlier 2026 increases. [9] Effective market pricing should nevertheless decline as neocloud supply expands and long-term discounts deepen.

The key distinction is between GPU-hour price and cost per useful token. The latter should fall faster, favoring inference platforms with superior utilization and software efficiency rather than operators owning the largest nominal fleet.

...

- B200 availability and HBM/CoWoS pricing: the earliest signal of whether next-generation supply can relieve premium-GPU scarcity.
- Neocloud utilization and financing: aggressive discounts are sustainable only if power, depreciation, and debt-service costs remain covered.
- Inference utilization thresholds: sustained utilization above 30–60% increasingly determines whether self-hosted deployments beat API pricing.

...

results.title: The Price of a GPU-Hour Is Now Set by Memory, Not Compute | AIChieve
results.author: Jorge Fernandez Ilufi
highlights:
Cloud provider Nebius raised its hourly rate for an Nvidia H100 chip from $3.85 to $4.50 on October 1, 2026, while pushing the newer B200 to $8.50. 

Cloud provider Nebius raised its hourly rate for an Nvidia H100 chip from $3.85 to $4.50 on October 1, 2026, while pushing the newer B200 to $8.50 [3]. The chips did not get faster, but their memory now costs much more. Two days prior, TrendForce raised its 2027 forecast for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to a 121% jump over this year’s prices [1].

...

- 121% — HBM price jump: TrendForce expects the blended price of high-bandwidth memory to rise 121% next year due to tight supply and a shift to the newest HBM4 grade [1].
- 17% to 21% — Nebius rate hike: The cloud provider raised H100 rates to $4.50, H200 to $5.40, B200 to $8.50, and B300 to $9.50 per GPU-hour on October 1, 2026 [3].
- $8.55 vs $14.24 — B200 spread: An independent tracker puts the median on-demand B200 at $8.55 an hour at dedicated GPU clouds and $14.24 at large hyperscalers [5].
- 10% to 15% — DRAM contracts: TrendForce expects standard DRAM contract prices to climb another 10% to 15% in the fourth quarter [2].

...

What strikes me is that the price of the newest chip relies entirely on how much memory it holds, not how much math it does. A September index tracking rental rates put the B200 at $8.01 an hour [4]. It reported the chip now costs 21% more per unit of compute than the older H100 [4].

That reverses a June trend when the B200 was 18% cheaper [4].

results.title: IndiaAI GPU providers to serve overseas clients
results.author: Chandra R. Srikanth
highlights:
The move follows concerns that demand for computing power in India is not yet sufficient to absorb the capacity being added under the government-backed programme.

Allowing companies to serve customers abroad would give them another source of revenue while the domestic market develops, a senior government official said.

"There is not enough uptake of GPUs in India right now. It is, therefore, important that these companies are able to sell the compute for the right price to anyone globally," the official said on condition of anonymity.

Under the Rs 10,372-crore IndiaAI Mission, the government has empanelled 14 companies to provide computing capacity using GPUs sourced from manufacturers including Nvidia, Intel and AMD.

The selected companies include Jio Platforms, Tata Communications and Yotta Data Services, alongside other data centre and cloud service providers.
